title: Cooking won't be replaced by AI: it's a reservation against the world of indirect experience
dek: Professional cooking and shrinking home cooking are irreversible trends, but taste cannot be replicated by data—so the kitchen stove becomes the last place where people can keep direct, embodied presence in the world of concepts.
why: A light bonus episode of casual conversation with moderate information density, but the discussion of embodied presence and palate pickiness, as well as the segment on AI cooking, is worth hearing; you can skip the rest.
who: Listeners interested in whether AI will replace cooking, and readers who want to understand eating from historical and sociological perspectives.
skip: You can skip the cooking chat at the start (0:00-4:17) and the knife-work and eating chat at the end (50:43-51:52) without losing the main argument.

points.h: The ‘firewood’in basics conceals a complete survival skillset
points.body: Li Yun points out that modern people struggle to understand why ancients put ‘firewood’ first in ‘firewood, rice, oil, salt’—today, lighting a stove is just turning a knob, but anciently, knowing which firewood catches easily was a skill even four- or five-year-olds had to master. Meng Qingyan adds his childhood camping experience: without alcohol blocks, using newspaper to kindle the firewood was exhausting, showing how the preliminary steps modern people skip cost the ancients tremendous effort.

points.h: Even Zhou royal kitchens had full-time cloth washers
points.body: Li Yun describes from the Rites of Zhou the division of labor in royal kitchens—three thousand years ago, Zhou courts employed a position called ‘秘人’ (cloth keepers) solely to clean the cloth covering food. He uses this to show that the king's court was where civilization accumulated densest, where eating was most elaborate and meticulous, and thus where dietary practices left behind recordable traces, while ordinary people's eating habits remain obscure for want of documentation.

points.h: Home cooking will shrink but professional cooking won't disappear
points.body: Meng Qingyan raises that food delivery platforms created ‘an unprecedented separation of eating from cooking in human history’—anciently, food and cooking costs consumed 70-90% of income, but that share has collapsed. Li Yun concludes: by pure efficiency of nutrition and satiation, home cooking ‘is a bad deal,’ so it will keep shrinking, but as long as people eat, cooking itself—social and professional cooking—won't vanish.

points.h: Why people cook differs; there is no single answer
points.body: Meng Qingyan explains his motive is ‘瘫嘴’—food delivery tastes monotonous day after day, so he cooks to break the taste monotony and to recreate his parents' cooking from childhood. He notes that another friend, He Bi (何必), cooks for an opposite reason: He Bi's mind is typically scattered, but cooking requires his full attention—inattention burns the dish. They conclude: each person's reason for cooking differs, which is precisely how modern life requires people to find their own meaning.

points.h: Would robots taking over cooking completely be good?
points.body: Li Yun poses a hypothesis: if humanoid robots mastered all cooking skills and entirely replaced humans at cooking, would that be desirable? His answer is no—the more advanced AI becomes, the more human embodied ability and sensation gets ‘carved away,’ and people might end up living narrower lives. He presses further: AI can read and speak, but ‘can it recognize taste?’ Even if AI judges flavor, that judgment bears no necessary relation to whether ‘I’ myself can taste that flavor.

points.h: Spice level quantifies, but what spice tastes like to each person doesn't
points.body: They discuss the limits of AI and data-driven cooking: temperature, knife thickness, salt by the gram can be precisely replicated, but once ‘spice’ is assigned a value of one to one hundred, different people feel completely different things eating the same spicy dish—Li Yun's spice tolerance clearly exceeds Meng Qingyan's. Meng extends this deeper: when he cooks saltier, friends still eat it and taste ‘heavy mouth,’ because ‘my cooking is me’—the cook brings mood and their day's state into the food, and that is precisely cooking's most unstandardizable part, as proved by a Tianjin small restaurant owner's remark: ‘if my mood is bad, maybe I didn't perform well.’

points.h: Cooking is the reservation against the world of indirect experience
points.body: Meng Qingyan proposes: history is the future. From history's trend of labor specialization and delegated convenience, the process is irreversible, but cooking's meaning might lie precisely in preserving human embodied presence—the direct connection between person and world, nature, and time. He cites unfollowing travel influencers as an example: when video capture technology is so strong that visiting in person doesn't compare to the screen, this challenge to embodied presence becomes increasingly common, and cooking as the most accessible direct experience in daily life might become the smallest unit of resistance against this trend.

points.h: Neither embrace nor resist AI—it becomes infrastructure
points.body: Meng Qingyan responds to He Bi's earlier question whether he is a ‘embracer’ or ‘resister’: he is neither, because AI technology will, like DOS becoming Windows or handwriting becoming Word, gradually become life's default and infrastructure over time—this cannot be resisted. Meanwhile, he has followed many cooks' short videos, especially how avant-garde chefs' imaginative approaches often make him think ‘you can do it like that?,’ showing that AI and new tools can open more techniques and imagination for cooking, not just threaten embodied presence.

terms.def: Direct experience where the body participates and perceives the world, in contrast to indirect experience on screens.

quotes.text: I leaned on this for a while—where does this fuel come from? Um, do you have to go out and cut firewood? Um, what size should firewood be cut to so it burns easily? Actually, for the ancients, all these things were essential skills.
But you see, besides being lazy, I have this other thing—I'm pickish about taste. I'm someone who is both lazy and pickish about taste.
But I think there's something really troublesome: now AI can recognize writing—it recognizes it well, speaks it well—but can it recognize taste?
He wants you, in a sense, not to eat the food he made, but to know who the person cooking for you is—to understand what kind of person they really are.
I say I neither embrace nor resist. What's there to embrace or resist—as if your resistance could actually stop it?
